module.title: Quantitative Foundations II — Functions & Precalculus
module.destination: From reliable algebra, become fluent with functions as objects, legal domains/ranges, graphs and transformations, finite indexed models, exponential/logarithmic reasoning, log returns and the minimal trigonometry needed by later quantitative work.
module.gate: M02 is not cleared by page completion. Publication requires semantic ancestry, prerequisite-symbol audit, novice instruction, claim coverage, independent math/reference validation, evidence integrity and browser validation.
module.nextBoundary: M03 owns proof habits, logic, sets/maps and combinatorics. M09 owns limits, convergence and infinite-series arguments. M02 must not certify either family.
module.acceptance: Previous author-validation superseded by bounded independent review M02-01 through M02-04; reaccept only after green gates.

owns: finite arithmetic/geometric sequences and sigma notation
excludes: complex-number theory beyond later bounded bridges

sessions.title: Functions as input-output objects
sessions.focus: Function notation, inputs, outputs, rules and changed inputs.
sessions.purpose: Turn formulas from static algebra into reusable mappings before graphs, models and composition.
sessions.centralCapability: Evaluate a function at numerical and symbolic inputs, distinguish rule/input/output, and build a simple rule from a verbal relationship.
sessions.principalObstacle: Learners often treat f(x) as f times x or replace only part of a changed input.
requiredOwnership: Interpret f(x) as the output assigned to input x.
Substitute an entire numerical or symbolic input with parentheses when needed.
Distinguish a function rule from one evaluated output.
Identify independent input and dependent output in context.
Translate a simple verbal input-output rule into function notation.
sessions.applicationScope: Elementary real-valued functions and finite quantitative models.
sessions.transferScope: A fresh representation or model requiring the same capability without naming the procedure.
outOfScope: Formal set-theoretic function definitions reserved for M03
sessions.exitCondition: Evaluate one unfamiliar changed-input expression and write one contextual function rule with input/output roles stated.
sessions.lesson: A function is a rule that assigns one output to each legal input. The notation f(x) names the output, not multiplication. Replace the whole input slot: if g(u)=2u+5, then g(a−1)=2(a−1)+5=2a+3. Worked example: for g(u)=2u+5, g(4)=13 and g(−3)=−1. Guided check: if H(t)=7−3t, find H(2), H(z+2), and say which symbol is the input.

sessions.title: Domains, ranges & legal inputs
sessions.focus: Natural domains, denominator/root restrictions and simple ranges.
sessions.purpose: Make legal-input reasoning automatic before composition, logs, rational functions and data models.
sessions.centralCapability: Determine a real domain from algebraic restrictions and determine simple ranges from elementary structure or a stated restricted domain.
sessions.principalObstacle: A simplified formula can hide excluded inputs, and square-root/denominator conditions are often applied incompletely.
requiredOwnership: Exclude denominator zeros from the original expression.
Require even-root radicands to be nonnegative.
Strengthen a root condition to strict positivity when the root is in a denominator.
Intersect simultaneous domain restrictions.
Determine a simple range from an elementary graph/algebraic restriction.
sessions.applicationScope: Elementary real-valued functions and finite quantitative models.
sessions.transferScope: A fresh representation or model requiring the same capability without naming the procedure.
sessions.exitCondition: State the exact domain of one mixed root/rational expression and the range of one elementary restricted function.
sessions.lesson: A domain is the set of legal inputs; a range is the set of outputs the legal inputs can actually attain. Denominators cannot be zero. For a real principal square root, the radicand must be ≥0; if that square root is itself a denominator, it must be >0. Intersect all input restrictions. To find a simple range, bound the output and check the bound is attainable. Worked example: r(x)=√(x−1)/(x+4) requires x≥1, so its domain is [1,∞). Separately, q(x)=x² on −1≤x≤3 has minimum0 (attained at x=0) and maximum9 (attained at x=3), so its range is [0,9]. If legal outputs occur in disconnected pieces, ∪ means union: y≤−2 or y≥1 is (−∞,−2]∪[1,∞). Guided check: find the domain of 1/√(9−y), then find the range of z² on −1≤z≤4 and justify both endpoints.

sessions.title: Graphs, coordinates & geometric reading
sessions.focus: Graphs as input-output point sets, intercepts, tables, distance and midpoint.
sessions.purpose: Build visual/coordinate fluency before slope, transformations and later empirical plots.
sessions.centralCapability: Translate among rule, table and graph points; identify intercepts; and compute elementary coordinate distance/midpoint.
sessions.principalObstacle: A graph is often treated as a picture disconnected from the function values it represents.
requiredOwnership: Interpret (x,f(x)) as a graph point.
Build a finite value table from a rule.
Identify x- and y-intercepts algebraically.
Compute distance between two coordinate points.
Compute the midpoint of two coordinate points.
sessions.applicationScope: Elementary real-valued functions and finite quantitative models.
sessions.transferScope: A fresh representation or model requiring the same capability without naming the procedure.
outOfScope: Slope as a model parameter until S04
sessions.exitCondition: From one unfamiliar rule, produce points/intercepts and one exact distance or midpoint calculation.
sessions.lesson: The graph of y=f(x) consists of points (x,f(x)). A y-intercept uses x=0; an x-intercept solves f(x)=0. For points (x₁,y₁),(x₂,y₂), distance is √[(x₂−x₁)²+(y₂−y₁)²] and midpoint averages coordinates. Worked example: y=x+2 has intercepts (−2,0),(0,2). Guided check: tabulate y=x²−1 at x=−1,0,2 and find the distance between the first two graph points.

sessions.title: Linear functions, slope & units
sessions.focus: Slope as change per input unit, intercepts and line equations.
sessions.purpose: Prepare quantitative model interpretation, local change intuition and later regression.
sessions.centralCapability: Recover and interpret a linear function from points or slope/intercept information, carrying units through slope.
sessions.principalObstacle: Slope is memorized as a fraction without interpreting numerator/denominator units or checking consistency.
requiredOwnership: Compute slope Δy/Δx from two distinct-x points.
Interpret slope units as output units per input unit.
Write a line equation from two points or a point and slope.
Identify intercept meaning in a context.
Use a linear model forward and backward.
sessions.applicationScope: Elementary real-valued functions and finite quantitative models.
sessions.transferScope: A fresh representation or model requiring the same capability without naming the procedure.
sessions.exitCondition: Build and interpret one line from data points, including slope units and one inverse-use calculation.
sessions.lesson: For a line, slope m=(y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁) is output change per input change. Once m is known, y=mx+b and one point determines b. Worked example: through (1,4),(5,12), m=2 and y=2x+2. Guided check: find the line through (−2,7),(4,−5), state slope units generically, and verify both points.

sessions.title: Piecewise functions & absolute-value graphs
sessions.focus: Branch conditions, boundary inclusion and piecewise representations.
sessions.purpose: Prepare for threshold rules, transaction costs and later piecewise models.
sessions.centralCapability: Evaluate and describe a piecewise function at boundaries and convert a basic absolute-value rule to piecewise form.
sessions.principalObstacle: Learners often apply the wrong branch at an endpoint or ignore branch conditions after simplification.
requiredOwnership: Choose the correct branch from its stated condition.
Handle included/excluded boundary points exactly.
Compute a piecewise function range in an elementary case.
Rewrite |x−a| as two linear branches.
Interpret the vertex/range of a translated absolute-value graph.
sessions.applicationScope: Elementary real-valued functions and finite quantitative models.
sessions.transferScope: A fresh representation or model requiring the same capability without naming the procedure.
sessions.exitCondition: Evaluate a new piecewise rule at boundary-adjacent inputs and convert one shifted absolute value into correct branches.
sessions.lesson: A piecewise function is one function with different rules on different input regions. The condition chooses the rule. For |x−a|, values left of a use a−x and values at/right use x−a. Worked example: |x−1|={1−x for x<1; x−1 for x≥1}. Guided check: evaluate a two-branch rule at the boundary and rewrite |x+4| piecewise.

sessions.title: Graph transformations & parameters
sessions.focus: Shifts, reflections, stretches/compressions and transformed domains/ranges.
sessions.purpose: Make parameter effects predictable before modeling, trig graphs and local approximations.
sessions.centralCapability: Read a transformed function from a base graph/rule and determine key points, domain/range and parameter effects.
sessions.principalObstacle: Horizontal changes act inside the input and are commonly given the wrong direction.
requiredOwnership: Interpret f(x−h)+k as a horizontal/vertical shift.
Interpret −f(x) and f(−x) as reflections.
Interpret vertical scaling af(x).
Track domain/range through elementary transformations.
Read key geometric features from a transformed standard function.
sessions.applicationScope: Elementary real-valued functions and finite quantitative models.
sessions.transferScope: A fresh representation or model requiring the same capability without naming the procedure.
sessions.exitCondition: Describe and verify one unfamiliar transformation sequence and recover domain/range/key point.
sessions.lesson: Changes outside f act on outputs; changes inside act on inputs. For q(x)=(x+2)²−4, the x² graph shifts left2 and down4. Multiplying outputs by −1 reflects across the x-axis. Worked example: y=3(x+1)²−2 has vertex(−1,−2). Guided check: describe y=−(x−4)²+7 and state its vertex and range.

sessions.title: Composition & changed-input domains
sessions.focus: f∘g, order sensitivity and legal-input tracing.
sessions.purpose: Prepare nested models, data pipelines and later chain-rule thinking without calculus.
sessions.centralCapability: Compute compositions in both orders and determine their domains from the inner output and outer-input restrictions.
sessions.principalObstacle: Composition is mistaken for multiplication or treated as commutative.
requiredOwnership: Compute (f∘g)(x)=f(g(x)).
Compute both composition orders without assuming equality.
Track the inner function output into the outer domain.
State exact composition domains in elementary rational cases.
Evaluate a composition at a specific input as a check.
sessions.applicationScope: Elementary real-valued functions and finite quantitative models.
sessions.transferScope: A fresh representation or model requiring the same capability without naming the procedure.
sessions.exitCondition: Compute both orders for an unfamiliar pair and give the correct domain of each.
sessions.lesson: In f∘g, g acts first and its output becomes f's input. Order matters. Worked example: f(x)=x+4,g(x)=3x gives f(g(x))=3x+4 but g(f(x))=3x+12. Guided check: compose f(x)=x² and g(x)=x−2 in both orders and compare at x=3.

sessions.title: One-to-one functions & inverses
sessions.focus: Inverse functions, domain/range swapping and needed restrictions.
sessions.purpose: Prepare log/exponential inversion, quantile ideas and reversible model transformations.
sessions.centralCapability: Decide elementary one-to-one behavior, construct an inverse by solving y=f(x), and verify domain/range/compositions.
sessions.principalObstacle: The symbol f⁻¹ is confused with 1/f, and non-one-to-one rules are inverted without restricting the domain.
requiredOwnership: Distinguish inverse function notation from reciprocal notation.
Construct an inverse of a one-to-one elementary function.
Swap domain/range correctly between a function and inverse.
Recognize why x² on R has no function inverse.
Restrict a standard non-one-to-one function to obtain an inverse.
sessions.applicationScope: Elementary real-valued functions and finite quantitative models.
sessions.transferScope: A fresh representation or model requiring the same capability without naming the procedure.
outOfScope: Formal injective/surjective proofs reserved for M03
sessions.exitCondition: Construct and verify one inverse and repair one non-invertible standard function by an explicit domain restriction.
sessions.lesson: An inverse reverses input and output. Write y=f(x), solve for x, then rename. f⁻¹ is not 1/f. A function needs one-to-one behavior on its chosen domain. Worked example: f(x)=5x+2 has f⁻¹(y)=(y−2)/5. Guided check: invert h(x)=(x−4)/3 and verify both compositions.

sessions.title: Polynomial functions: zeros, multiplicity & shape
sessions.focus: Degree, leading term, factored zeros and crossing/touching behavior.
sessions.purpose: Prepare algebraic models, characteristic polynomials and later local/global analysis.
sessions.centralCapability: Read degree, leading behavior, zeros and elementary multiplicity effects from a factored polynomial.
sessions.principalObstacle: A repeated factor is treated like an ordinary crossing and leading behavior is ignored.
requiredOwnership: Identify polynomial degree and leading coefficient.
Read zeros from a factored polynomial.
Identify zero multiplicity from repeated factors.
Distinguish odd-multiplicity crossing from even-multiplicity touching in elementary graphs.
Infer left/right end behavior from degree parity and leading sign.
sessions.applicationScope: Elementary real-valued functions and finite quantitative models.
sessions.transferScope: A fresh representation or model requiring the same capability without naming the procedure.
sessions.exitCondition: From one factored polynomial, state degree, zeros/multiplicities and a coherent qualitative graph description.
sessions.lesson: In factored form, each factor x−r gives zero r; its exponent is the multiplicity. Odd multiplicity changes sign through the zero; even multiplicity keeps the local sign. The leading term determines far-left/far-right direction. Worked example: (x+2)²(x−4) has degree3, double zero−2 and simple zero4. Guided check: analyze −(x−1)³(x+5) for degree, zeros, multiplicities and end directions.

sessions.title: Rational functions: holes, exclusions & asymptotic shape
sessions.focus: Original domains, cancellation holes, denominator poles and large-x leading ratios.
sessions.purpose: Prevent illegal cancellation/domain loss before likelihoods, transfer functions and data normalizations.
sessions.centralCapability: Simplify a rational function while retaining original exclusions and distinguish removable holes from nonremovable denominator singularities.
sessions.principalObstacle: Cancellation is treated as erasing an excluded input, making two formulas falsely identical as functions.
requiredOwnership: Factor numerator/denominator before cancellation.
Retain every exclusion from the original denominator.
Identify a cancelled denominator zero as a hole.
Identify a remaining denominator zero as a vertical singularity/asymptote in elementary cases.
Use leading-degree/coefficient comparison for elementary large-|x| horizontal behavior.
sessions.applicationScope: Elementary real-valued functions and finite quantitative models.
sessions.transferScope: A fresh representation or model requiring the same capability without naming the procedure.
sessions.exitCondition: Audit one unfamiliar rational function with a cancellation and state its domain, hole and remaining asymptotic features.
sessions.lesson: A cancellation gives an equivalent formula only on the original domain. A cancelled denominator factor leaves a hole; a denominator zero that remains produces an unbounded vertical feature in these elementary examples. Equal top/bottom degree gives horizontal large-|x| level from leading-coefficient ratio. Worked example: (x²−9)/(x²−x−6) reduces to (x+3)/(x+2), while x=3 remains a hole and x=−2 remains excluded. Guided check: factor (x²+x−6)/(x²−4) and classify its excluded inputs.

sessions.title: Root & power functions
sessions.focus: Fractional powers, transformed roots, domains/ranges and simple equations.
sessions.purpose: Connect M01 exponent mechanics to function families used in scaling laws and transformations.
sessions.centralCapability: Analyze elementary root/power functions for legal real inputs, ranges and simple inverse equations.
sessions.principalObstacle: Rational exponents are manipulated without checking real-domain restrictions or principal-root sign.
requiredOwnership: Determine domains of translated/scaled even-root functions.
Determine simple ranges from principal-root structure.
Evaluate simple rational powers with odd roots.
Handle reciprocal-root strict domain restrictions.
Solve a simple root-function equation and check the result.
sessions.applicationScope: Elementary real-valued functions and finite quantitative models.
sessions.transferScope: A fresh representation or model requiring the same capability without naming the procedure.
sessions.exitCondition: Analyze one transformed root function and one reciprocal/rational-power function without losing domain conditions.
sessions.lesson: A root function carries its root-domain rule everywhere. For √(ax+b), require ax+b≥0; if the root is downstairs, require >0. Odd roots accept negative inputs. Worked example: y=√(3−x) has domain x≤3 and range y≥0. Guided check: find domain/range of √(2x+8)−4 and evaluate (−27)^(2/3).

sessions.title: Exponential functions: growth & decay
sessions.focus: Positive-base exponential models, per-step multipliers and graph behavior.
sessions.purpose: Prepare compounding, log inversion, decay models and later stochastic growth notation.
sessions.centralCapability: Interpret and evaluate A·b^t models, linking base b to per-unit multiplicative growth or decay.
sessions.principalObstacle: The base is confused with an additive change and percentages are added across periods instead of compounded.
requiredOwnership: Recognize b>1 as growth and 0<b<1 as decay.
Interpret b as the multiplier per one input unit.
Translate a percent growth/decay rate to an exponential base.
Evaluate an exponential model at integer inputs.
Identify initial value from t=0.
sessions.applicationScope: Elementary real-valued functions and finite quantitative models.
sessions.transferScope: A fresh representation or model requiring the same capability without naming the procedure.
sessions.exitCondition: Build/evaluate one growth or decay model and explain its per-step multiplier and initial value.
sessions.lesson: In A·b^t, A is the t=0 value and b is the multiplier for each +1 in t. Eight-percent growth uses b=1.08; twelve-percent decay uses b=0.88. Worked example: 200(1.05)^t starts at200 and multiplies by1.05 per period. Guided check: interpret and evaluate 900(0.92)^t at t=0,1,2.

sessions.title: Logarithms as inverse exponentials
sessions.focus: log_b y=x iff b^x=y, natural logs and log domains.
sessions.purpose: Create the inverse language needed for growth equations, log returns and later likelihoods.
sessions.centralCapability: Translate exactly between logarithmic and exponential statements, evaluate elementary logs and enforce positive log arguments.
sessions.principalObstacle: Logs are treated as a button rather than an inverse function with a strict positive-input domain.
requiredOwnership: Use log_b(y)=x iff b^x=y.
State base conditions b>0,b≠1.
Evaluate elementary exact logarithms.
Recognize ln as log base e.
Require every real logarithm argument to be positive.
sessions.applicationScope: Elementary real-valued functions and finite quantitative models.
sessions.transferScope: A fresh representation or model requiring the same capability without naming the procedure.
sessions.exitCondition: Convert and evaluate unfamiliar elementary log statements and state a correct log-function domain.
sessions.lesson: log_b(y) asks: what exponent on b gives y? Thus log_b(y)=x exactly when b^x=y, with b>0,b≠1 and y>0. ln is base e. Worked example: log₂8=3 because2³=8; log₁₀0.01=−2. Guided check: evaluate log₅125 and state the domain of ln(7−x).

sessions.title: Log laws with domain discipline
sessions.focus: Products, quotients, powers and the legality of splitting real logs.
sessions.purpose: Prevent later likelihood/log-return algebra from silently changing domains.
sessions.centralCapability: Use log laws on legal positive factors and audit identities whose split form has a smaller domain.
sessions.principalObstacle: log(ab)=log a+log b is applied when a,b are individually negative or zero even though only the product is positive.
requiredOwnership: Use log(ab)=log a+log b when individual real logs are defined.
Use log(a/b)=log a−log b under positive-domain conditions.
Use log(a^k)=k log a under an explicitly legal base/argument condition.
Retain domain restrictions when expanding/condensing logs.
Use ln(x²)=2ln|x| for x≠0 rather than illegally assuming x>0.
sessions.applicationScope: Elementary real-valued functions and finite quantitative models.
sessions.transferScope: A fresh representation or model requiring the same capability without naming the procedure.
sessions.exitCondition: Simplify one legal log expression and repair one false identity by stating exact domains.
sessions.lesson: Real log laws are identities on their common legal domain. Splitting log(ab) into log a+log b requires a>0 and b>0, even though ab>0 could also happen with both negative. For x≠0, ln(x²)=2ln|x|. Worked example: for u,v>0, ln(9u²/v)=ln9+2lnu−lnv. Guided check: audit ln((z+2)²)=2ln(z+2) over the real line.

sessions.title: Exponential & logarithmic equations
sessions.focus: Same-base solving, taking logs and domain checks.
sessions.purpose: Enable exact time/parameter recovery in exponential models without guesswork.
sessions.centralCapability: Solve elementary exponential/log equations exactly, choosing same-base algebra or logarithms and checking domain restrictions.
sessions.principalObstacle: Taking logs is used mechanically without isolating a positive exponential expression or checking log-equation candidates.
requiredOwnership: Solve an exponential equation by matching bases when possible.
Take logs to solve a positive exponential equation when bases do not match.
Solve a one-log equation using inverse operations.
Solve a two-log equation with legal log algebra or an equivalent valid route.
Reject log-equation candidates that violate the original positive-argument domain.
sessions.applicationScope: Elementary real-valued functions and finite quantitative models.
sessions.transferScope: A fresh representation or model requiring the same capability without naming the procedure.
sessions.exitCondition: Solve one unfamiliar exponential and one logarithmic equation with exact-domain justification.
sessions.lesson: If bases match, equate exponents. Otherwise isolate the positive exponential and take logs: b^x=c gives x=ln c/ln b. For log equations, preserve positive arguments and check candidates. Worked example: 3·5^x=75 gives5^x=25, so x=2. Guided check: solve 2e^(0.3t)=9 exactly and solve ln(y+4)=ln12.

sessions.title: Growth time, compounding & log returns
sessions.focus: Discrete/continuous growth clocks and additive log returns.
sessions.purpose: Supply the exact logarithmic return language required by M07 markets without smuggling it into finance later.
sessions.centralCapability: Compute arithmetic and log returns, use log additivity across positive price ratios, and solve doubling times in discrete/continuous growth models.
sessions.principalObstacle: Arithmetic returns are added across periods and log returns are used without requiring positive prices.
requiredOwnership: Compute a one-period arithmetic return (P1−P0)/P0.
Compute log return ln(P1/P0) for positive prices.
Show consecutive log returns add to the total log return.
Compute cumulative simple return from endpoint prices.
Solve doubling time for A e^(rt) and A(1+g)^t.
sessions.applicationScope: Elementary real-valued functions and finite quantitative models.
sessions.transferScope: A fresh representation or model requiring the same capability without naming the procedure.
sessions.exitCondition: Given a short positive price path and a growth model, compute both return types and an exact doubling time.
sessions.lesson: For positive prices, simple return is P₁/P₀−1; log return is ln(P₁/P₀). Consecutive log returns add because log ratios telescope. In Ae^(rt), doubling solves e^(rt)=2. Worked example: 50→55 has simple return10% and log return ln1.1. Guided check: for 200→180→198, compute both simple period returns and show the two log returns sum to ln(198/200).

sessions.title: Arithmetic sequences & finite sums
sessions.focus: Indexing, common difference, nth terms and finite AP sums.
sessions.purpose: Prepare indexed data/time steps and finite series before convergence is introduced later.
sessions.centralCapability: Model and solve finite arithmetic sequences with explicit indexing and finite-sum formulas.
sessions.principalObstacle: Off-by-one errors arise when the first term and index origin are not stated.
requiredOwnership: Treat a sequence as a function on integer indices.
Use a_n=a_1+(n−1)d with stated indexing.
Recover d and a_1 from two indexed terms.
Compute a requested finite arithmetic term.
Compute a finite arithmetic sum without invoking infinite-series ideas.
sessions.applicationScope: Elementary real-valued functions and finite quantitative models.
sessions.transferScope: A fresh representation or model requiring the same capability without naming the procedure.
sessions.exitCondition: Recover an arithmetic sequence from indexed data and compute an unfamiliar term and finite sum.
sessions.lesson: An arithmetic sequence adds the same difference d each step. With first term a₁, a_n=a₁+(n−1)d. The finite sum is n(a₁+a_n)/2. Worked example: a₁=5,d=3 gives a₆=20 and S₆=75. Guided check: if a₃=11 and a₇=27, recover d and a₁.

sessions.title: Geometric sequences & finite geometric sums
sessions.focus: Constant ratios, nth terms and finite GP sums including r=1.
sessions.purpose: Prepare compounding, discounted cashflows and finite weighted sums without premature infinite-series claims.
sessions.centralCapability: Compute terms and finite sums of geometric sequences with explicit treatment of the r=1 branch.
sessions.principalObstacle: The finite-sum formula is used with wrong indexing or division by 1−r when r=1.
requiredOwnership: Identify a constant ratio r.
Use g_n=g_1 r^(n−1).
Compute a finite geometric sum for r≠1.
Handle r=1 separately.
Check a finite sum against term scale/count.
sessions.applicationScope: Elementary real-valued functions and finite quantitative models.
sessions.transferScope: A fresh representation or model requiring the same capability without naming the procedure.
sessions.exitCondition: Compute one unfamiliar finite geometric sequence term/sum and state the exceptional r=1 formula.
sessions.lesson: A geometric sequence multiplies by a constant ratio r. With first term g₁, g_n=g₁r^(n−1). For r≠1, the finite-sum formula can be reconstructed by subtraction: S_n=g₁+g₁r+…+g₁r^(n−1); then rS_n=g₁r+…+g₁r^n, so S_n−rS_n=g₁−g₁r^n and S_n=g₁(1−r^n)/(1−r). For r=1, division by1−r is illegal and S_n=ng₁. Worked example: 5,15,45,… has r=3 and S₄=200. Guided check: infer the ratio of 64,32,16,… then find its sixth term and first-six sum, checking against the explicit terms.

sessions.title: Sigma notation & finite indexed sums
sessions.focus: Σ notation, bounds, reindexing and finite arithmetic/geometric expressions.
sessions.purpose: Create compact notation used everywhere in probability, statistics, linear algebra and objectives.
sessions.centralCapability: Read, expand, evaluate and reindex finite sigma expressions without off-by-one errors.
sessions.principalObstacle: Lower/upper bounds are ignored or the index is treated as a fixed unknown rather than a running placeholder.
requiredOwnership: Read lower/upper sigma bounds and count terms.
Expand a finite sigma expression into terms.
Evaluate a finite sigma exactly.
Write an explicit finite pattern in sigma notation.
Reindex a finite sum while preserving the same terms.
sessions.applicationScope: Elementary real-valued functions and finite quantitative models.
sessions.transferScope: A fresh representation or model requiring the same capability without naming the procedure.
sessions.exitCondition: Move both directions between finite sigma notation and an explicit list, including one correct reindexing.
sessions.lesson: Σ tells an index to run through stated integer values. Expand a few terms before applying formulas; the bounds are part of the object. Worked example: Σ(k=1..4)(k+2)=3+4+5+6=18. Guided check: write 2+5+8+11+14 as a sigma sum and reindex Σ(j=3..6)j to start at0.

sessions.title: Recurrences, iteration & fixed-point candidates
sessions.focus: One-step recurrences, seed dependence and fixed-point equations without convergence shortcuts.
sessions.purpose: Prepare M09 limits and later dynamic programming while inoculating against L=f(L) as a convergence proof.
sessions.centralCapability: Generate recurrence terms, solve algebraic fixed-point candidates and clearly separate that calculation from proving convergence.
sessions.principalObstacle: A learner solves L=f(L) and immediately declares that every recurrence converges to L.
requiredOwnership: Generate terms from a stated seed and recurrence.
Interpret recurrence as repeated application of a function.
Solve L=f(L) for a fixed-point candidate.
State that a fixed-point equation alone does not prove convergence.
Use an explicit recurrence example to refute an unjustified convergence claim.
sessions.applicationScope: Elementary real-valued functions and finite quantitative models.
sessions.transferScope: A fresh representation or model requiring the same capability without naming the procedure.
sessions.exitCondition: Compute terms/fixed points for one recurrence and correctly state what has and has not been proved about long-run behavior.
sessions.lesson: A recurrence plus a seed defines terms step by step. A fixed point L satisfies L=f(L), but solving that equation only identifies a possible stationary value; it does not prove x_n approaches it. Worked example: x_{n+1}=x_n/3+2 has fixed point3. Guided check: generate four terms of y_{n+1}=−y_n with y0=1 and compare with its fixed point.

sessions.title: Angles, radians & the unit circle
sessions.focus: Degree/radian conversion, arc length and cosine/sine coordinates.
sessions.purpose: Provide the minimal geometric language later calculus, oscillations and periodic time series require.
sessions.centralCapability: Convert angle units, locate standard unit-circle angles and use radians in arc-length calculations.
sessions.principalObstacle: Radians are treated as arbitrary units rather than the dimensionless ratio arc length/radius.
requiredOwnership: Convert degrees to radians and back.
Interpret θ radians as arc length divided by radius.
Use s=rθ for oriented arc displacement when θ is in radians.
Read (cosθ,sinθ) from the unit circle at standard angles.
Determine signs from the quadrant.
sessions.applicationScope: Elementary real-valued functions and finite quantitative models.

sessions.lesson: Angles measure rotation. Positive angles turn counterclockwise and negative angles clockwise. In radians, θ=s/r: the signed angle is arc displacement divided by radius, so s=rθ. A full turn is2π radians=360°. On the unit circle the point is(cosθ,sinθ). The standard acute values come from two triangles: splitting an equilateral triangle gives cos60°=1/2, sin60°=√3/2 and therefore cos30°=√3/2, sin30°=1/2; an isosceles right triangle normalized to hypotenuse1 gives cos45°=sin45°=√2/2. For other quadrants, use the acute reference angle and then apply coordinate signs: I(+,+), II(−,+), III(−,−), IV(+,−). Worked example: 210° has reference angle30°, lies in III, and therefore has unit-circle coordinates(−√3/2,−1/2). Guided check: convert 300° to radians, identify its reference angle/quadrant, and find its coordinates.
